title: Epilepsy surgery for temporal lobe seizures
description: When temporal lobe seizures cannot be controlled with medicine, surgery to remove or destroy the area where they start (including by laser) can stop them; about two thirds of people become seizure-free. One study scanned people before and, on average, about three years after surgery. In those who became seizure-free, two of the brainstem's arousal centres, which keep the brain awake and alert, became more in step with the cortex, looking more like people without epilepsy. Lines show how closely areas work together: in the first part compared with people without epilepsy (dashed means less); in "What changed" compared with before surgery (pulsing means more).
caveat: All findings come from one study of 15 people with temporal lobe epilepsy, 10 of whom became seizure-free, and 15 people without epilepsy; the authors call it a preliminary analysis. In the 5 who still had seizures no change was detected, but that group was very small. The weaker connections before surgery rest mainly on this group's earlier work. A third arousal centre, the ventral tegmental area, did not change. The arousal centres that changed are two small nuclei in the upper brainstem, drawn as the brainstem outline. The cortex areas are mapped approximately: the inferior frontal gyrus to the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, the precentral gyrus to the motor cortex, the postcentral gyrus to the sensory cortex. The superior parietal lobule is not in the brain model. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: Before surgery, the brainstem arousal centres are less in step with the cortex than in people without epilepsy, as this group found in earlier work.

phases.name: Surgery and recovery
phases.caption: Surgery, then at least a year, about three on average, before the second scan. The brain is drawn at rest here.
